meta.title: Who really said "When a person can't find a deep sense of meaning, they distract themselves with pleasure"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in Man's Search for Meaning. A full-text check of Frankl's book finds no such line — the idea is genuinely his, but the wording is a modern paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When a person can't find a deep sense of meaning, they distract themselves with pleasure'?
meta.ogDescription: A full-text search of Frankl's book returns zero hits for this sentence. What he actually wrote about the "existential vacuum" was sharper — and sourced.

answer.label: Not Frankl’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1905–1997 · Austrian neurologist, psychiatrist and founder of logotherapy
answer.sourceLine: The thought is authentically Frankl’s, but this sentence is not. A full-text search of Man’s Search for Meaning — the book this line is almost always pinned to — returns zero hits for “deep sense of meaning” and zero for “distract themselves.” What Frankl actually wrote, in his section on the “existential vacuum,” is that “the place of frustrated will to meaning is taken by the will to pleasure.” The popular line is a smoothed-out compression of that passage, and no source has ever been documented for it.

source.heading: What Frankl actually wrote

source.excerpt: Frankl’s own account of this idea runs through the term he coined for it, the “existential vacuum.” Where the will to meaning is frustrated, he writes, it is vicariously compensated for — sometimes by a will to power, and in other cases “the place of frustrated will to meaning is taken by the will to pleasure.”
trail: The line spreads chiefly from a Goodreads quote page ↗ that names no book, no page and no year — and that carries Goodreads’ own notice that community-added quotes are unverified. Other aggregators repeat it with the source field still blank ↗.

Checked against the book itself: a search of the full text of the Beacon Press edition of Man’s Search for Meaning finds no occurrence of “deep sense of meaning,” “distract themselves” or “distracts himself.” The genuine passage, reproduced here from Part Two ↗, makes the same argument in Frankl’s own terms.

No specialist has ruled on this one. Quote Investigator’s Frankl file ↗ covers the Nietzsche “why/how” line and the “between stimulus and response” quote, but not this sentence, and it is absent from Wikiquote’s sourced Frankl page ↗ as well.
Readers who want to check the passage in the book can consult the scanned 1984 Washington Square Press revised edition ↗ at the Internet Archive.
source.cutTag: Part Two · Logotherapy in a Nutshell
source.excerptNote: That last clause is the closest thing in the book to the popular quotation. The circulating sentence compresses it, drops the alternative substitutes Frankl names alongside pleasure, and replaces his clinical vocabulary with everyday phrasing.

source.rightsNote: The genuine passage quoted above is from Man’s Search for Meaning, whose Beacon Press edition carries copyright dates of 1959, 1962, 1984 and 1992 — all well after 1931, so the English text is firmly in copyright in the United States, as is Ilse Lasch’s translation of Part One. The popular paraphrase is a separate matter: because no source for it has ever been documented, its own status cannot be settled, and it should not be treated as free to reuse.

author.name: Viktor Frankl
author.heading: The man who actually made this argument
author.metaLine: 1905–1997 · Austrian neurologist, psychiatrist and founder of logotherapy
author.bio: Viktor Frankl was an Austrian neurologist and psychiatrist who founded logotherapy, often called the “Third Viennese School of Psychotherapy” after Freud’s and Adler’s. He survived Theresienstadt, Auschwitz and two further camps, and drew on that experience in Man’s Search for Meaning, first published in German in 1946 and in English in 1959. His central claim inverted Freud: the primary human drive is not the will to pleasure but the will to meaning — and where that will is frustrated, he argued, pleasure and power rush in to fill the void.

misattribution.heading: How a real idea got a fake sentence
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a quote pinned on the wrong person. Frankl really did argue that pleasure fills the space left by absent meaning — the attribution fails on the words, not the thinking. Three things mark it as a paraphrase rather than a quotation.

items.why: Searching the full text of the Beacon Press edition of Man’s Search for Meaning returns no instance of “deep sense of meaning” and no instance of “distract themselves.” The one appearance of “distracted” in the whole book describes a man excusing himself for being tired. Frankl’s actual text on the existential vacuum ↗ uses his own technical vocabulary throughout.

The book is named constantly in social posts sharing the line, but never with a page. The Goodreads entry ↗ that anchors most of the sharing cites no work at all, and carries the site’s standing notice that community-submitted quotes are not verified.

Goodreads separately hosts “When man can’t find meaning in his life, he distracts himself with pleasure” ↗, also unsourced, and the line circulates elsewhere with “a man” swapped for “a person.” A sentence copied from a printed page does not drift like this; a remembered idea does.

misattribution.truthLine: Frankl’s own sentence is more specific and more interesting: pleasure is only one of the “masks and guises” of the existential vacuum, alongside the will to power and the will to money — as he set out in Part Two of the book ↗.

context.heading: Why the real sentence is better than the fake one
lead: Frankl’s argument was a direct challenge to Freud. Where psychoanalysis put the pleasure principle at the base of human motivation, Frankl put the will to meaning — and he treated pleasure-seeking not as the engine but as the symptom, what rushes in once the search for meaning has failed. He gave the empty state a clinical name: the “existential vacuum,” which he said showed up mainly as boredom, and which he blamed for a run of modern ills from depression to addiction to what he called “Sunday neurosis.”

The paraphrase keeps that shape but sands off everything diagnostic about it. Frankl was describing a compensation mechanism he claimed to observe in patients, complete with a survey of his own students; the internet version turns it into a tidy aphorism about scrolling your phone. It is close enough to his meaning that people who have read the book nod along — which is exactly why it spread without anyone stopping to check the page number.
context.detailsSummary: What Frankl actually listed as the “masks and guises” of the vacuum
detailsBody: In the same passage Frankl names more than one substitute. The frustrated will to meaning, he writes, is sometimes compensated for by a will to power — including what he calls its most primitive form, the will to money. Only in other cases is its place taken by the will to pleasure.

That two-part structure is the first casualty of the paraphrase. The popular line offers pleasure as the single substitute for meaning; Frankl offered pleasure, power and money as alternative masks for the same underlying void.
context.pull: Frankl treated pleasure-seeking not as the engine of human behaviour but as what fills the space when meaning fails.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Goodreads page hosting this quote attributes it to Viktor E. Frankl but cites no source book, and states that community-added quotes are not verified by Goodreads.
Goodreads separately hosts the variant wording 'When man can't find meaning in his life, he distracts himself with pleasure', attributed to Frankl with no source book cited.
Quotepark shows the quote attributed to Viktor E. Frankl (1905-1997) with no source citation, inviting users to supply source information.

This extract of Frankl's own Part Two text contains 'In other cases, the place of frustrated will to meaning is taken by the will to pleasure' and 'Sometimes the frustrated will to meaning is vicariously compensated for by a will to power, including the most primitive form of the will to power, the will to money' — and contains neither 'distract themselves with pleasure' nor 'deep sense of meaning'.

Quote Investigator's Viktor E. Frankl category covers the 'why/how' quote and the 'between stimulus and response' quote, but has not investigated the 'deep sense of meaning / distract themselves with pleasure' line.

Wikiquote's Viktor Frankl page does not contain the quote 'When a person can't find a deep sense of meaning, they distract themselves with pleasure'; the page is organised around Man's Search for Meaning (1946; 1959; 1984).

Man's Search for Meaning was first published in German in 1946 as 'Ein Psychologe erlebt das Konzentrationslager' and first in English in 1959 by Beacon Press, with Ilse Lasch credited as translator of Part One.

Viktor Frankl lived 26 March 1905 to 2 September 1997, was an Austrian neurologist and psychiatrist, founded logotherapy (the 'Third Viennese School of Psychotherapy'), and survived Theresienstadt, Auschwitz and two other camps.
The Internet Archive holds a scanned copy of Man's Search for Meaning, catalogued as the 1984 revised edition published by Washington Square Press for Pocket Books.
